title: Rami bar Abba (II)
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: In Megillah 26b, while building a synagogue, he came before Rav Papa, who forbade it to him; before Rav Huna [son of Rav Yehoshua, as it should read], who answered him. Hyman reports that Dikdukei Soferim and Yuchasin read that he came before Rav Papi and R’ Huna bar Tachlifa. Hyman concludes that he was late according to all the readings.

It is possible that he was the father-in-law of Rav Ashi, as in Chullin 111a: ‘Rav Ashi came to the house of Rami bar Abba, his father-in-law; he saw his son roasting liver,’ etc. Hyman says, ‘We have already explained in the entry on Rav Ashi that it should read Rami bar Chama.’ But it is possible to say that he [Rav Ashi] had two wives. So is the reading of the She’iltot, Emor 72, that Rami bar Abba was Rav Ashi’s father-in-law, from Beitzah 29b; Hyman says, ‘Our reading there is Rami bar Chama.’ See the entry on R’ Ami bar Abba.

notes.text: The checked Megillah has Rav Huna forbidding the action as well, whereas the supplied summary merely says he answered. The two-wife explanation and the proposed Rami bar Chama reading remain Hyman’s possibilities.

All explicitly written Rav titles are retained locally, including Papa, Huna, Yehoshua, Papi and every Ashi occurrence. The distinct variant דר״ה is contextual Huna with title R-prime, not a transfer of full Rav from the earlier clause; the final Ami cross-reference also stays R-prime. The bracketed son-of-Rav-Yehoshua SHOULD READ is Hyman’s supplied emendation. His summary says Huna answered him; the previously reported Megillah prohibition is inherited only, not a newly read whole witness and not inserted into the summary. According to every reading he was late is Hyman’s compressed chronological judgment, not proof that he was the unique last sage. Hyman’s possible father-in-law relation, definite should-read Rami bar Chama argument in his Ashi entry, and possible two wives remain distinct claims, not admitted marriages or genealogy. The son in the liver quotation stays unresolved. Hyman’s first-person plural we have already explained and our reading are preserved with ownership. Sheiltot Emor 72, Chullin 111a and Beitzah 29b remain source locators; no new edition or printed history is verified. Both source holds remain.

In the consulted Megillah 26b, both Rav Papa and Rav Huna prohibit the action. The comparison table in Dikdukei Soferim (Megillah, reader p. 135, note ס) gives a manuscript line with Rav Huna [bar Tachlifa], retaining ‘and he said to him’. Yuchasin (London 1857, p. 128) lists Rav Huna bar Tachlifa, Rav Papi and Rami bar Abba together without narrating the consultation. Hyman gives a combined reading and his chronological conclusion. The consulted Chullin 111a–111b identifies the son in the liver episode as Rami bar Abba’s. Beitzah 29b names a daughter of Rami bar Chama, while the consulted Vilna 1861 She’iltot passage, digitally numbered 107, names a daughter of Rami bar Abba. The two-wife explanation remains Hyman’s conjecture.
